title: GAQAT: gradient-adaptive quantization-aware training for domain generalization
main_claims: Directly applying DG-SAM methods (e.g. SAGM) to quantized models causes severe performance degradation (up to 28.36% drop at 4-bit on PACS) due to gradient conflicts between task loss and smoothness loss in quantizer scaling factors.
A 'gradient disorder' metric can detect when scaling factor gradients are inconsistently directed across training steps, indicating sub-optimal convergence.
GAQAT's dynamic freezing strategy—selectively freezing scaling factor task gradients based on gradient disorder—stabilizes training and recovers near-full-precision OOD generalization.
methodology: SAGM's smoothness objective is incorporated into quantization-aware training by including scaling factors in the sharpness-aware perturbation. Gradient disorder is defined as the fraction of steps where gradient direction reverses sign. A dynamic algorithm selectively freezes scaling factor task gradients (gtask) for K steps when their disorder falls below threshold r. Experiments use LSQ-type QAT with ResNet-50 (MoCo-v2 pretrained) on PACS and DomainNet at 3-bit and 4-bit precision, following the DomainBed protocol.
key_results: GAQAT 4-bit achieves 61.33% average test accuracy on PACS, outperforming LSQ (58.98%) and SAGM+LSQ (56.93%) by up to 4.5%.
GAQAT 4-bit on DomainNet achieves 40.74%, near the full-precision baseline of 40.95%.
Reverse freezing (freezing high-disorder scaling factors) decreases performance, validating the gradient disorder indicator.
limitations: Only ResNet-50 is evaluated; generalizability to other architectures or higher-precision quantization is not studied.
Different domains in PACS show varying sensitivity to hyperparameters (freeze steps, threshold r), suggesting the method may need per-domain tuning.
The paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review.
relevance_to_rq: Peripheral: the paper applies SAM-based flatness optimization in the quantization setting, with limited relevance to the RQ's central comparison of SAM vs. SWA on CIFAR-C. However, it demonstrates that gradient conflicts (related to competing optimization objectives in SAM) can undermine OOD generalization—consistent with the RQ's interest in understanding what drives SAM's OOD gains.
